title: Learning from Errors and Failure in Educational Contexts https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bjep.12716 w-insights-and-future-directions-for-research-and-practice/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 3, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton's page summarizes a commentary by Narciss and Alemdag that synthesizes eleven research papers on learning from errors and failure across educational settings, organized around contextual factors like classroom climate, individual factors like motivation and emotion, error-related learning processes, and instructional strategies such as feedback. The commentary distinguishes conceptual challenges, including how to define an error versus a failure, from methodological ones, and uses both to chart future research directions. Its central practical thread is the idea of a positive error climate: a classroom culture where mistakes are discussed openly, without judgment, and treated as data to analyze rather than outcomes to punish. The piece also surveys specific instructional tools, rubrics, metacognitive prompts, deliberate errors, team error analysis, and dialogic peer assessment, that operationalize this climate in practice. It closes by calling for professional-development programs that build teachers' error competence and parallel programs to help parents support learning from mistakes at home.
points: A 'positive error climate,' where mistakes are discussed openly and without judgment, is presented as a precondition for students actually being able to learn from their errors.

Deliberate errors, asking students to intentionally make and then correct a mistake even when they know the answer, and team error analysis in group work are highlighted as concrete classroom techniques.
Instructional tools like rubrics and metacognitive prompts help students evaluate their own and peers' work and reflect on their learning process rather than just receive a correction.
Students respond to errors differently depending on age, self-worth, and emotion-regulation style, so instructional strategies for handling mistakes should be tailored rather than one-size-fits-all.
quotes: This commentary synthesizes eleven research papers exploring learning from errors and failures in educational settings.

The papers investigate contextual factors (e.g., classroom climate), individual factors (e.g., motivation and emotions), error-related learning processes, and instructional strategies (e.g., feedback) that influence learning.
Teachers should view errors not as failures, but as opportunities for growth.
Encourage deliberate errors by asking students to intentionally make and then correct mistakes, even when they know the answer.
One essential and preliminary condition for learning from errors might be a positive error climate in both formal and informal educational settings
